value.overview: The Inca Dove (Columbina inca) is a small, long-tailed dove of open and partly developed landscapes. Its gray-brown plumage has dark, scale-like markings, while the long tail shows white edges in flight. It usually walks on the ground while searching for seeds and often occurs near farms, villages, parks, and gardens. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species concentrated mainly in lowland and relatively dry areas, with some occurrence in the Central Valley.
value.classification: The Inca Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the genus Columbina. It is also called the Mexican Dove in parts of its range.
value.identification: This slender dove is about 20–23 cm long, with a long, narrow, square-ended tail and a finely scaled appearance created by dark feather edges. The body is gray-brown, the bill is dark, and the eye is reddish. Chest and belly tones can be faintly pinkish, especially in males. In flight, white outer tail feathers and warm chestnut underwings become conspicuous. Its small size, long tail, and overall scaly pattern help distinguish it from larger urban doves and shorter-tailed ground doves.
value.rangeHabitat: The Inca Dove ranges from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America to Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident, abundant in the northwestern lowlands, especially Guanacaste, and becomes less common southward along the Pacific lowlands, reaching at least the Quepos area. It is also common in parts of the Central Valley, with fewer records farther east. It favors open country, savannas, pastures, forest edges, secondary growth, towns, and suburbs, and generally avoids dense forest.
value.migrationStatus: The Inca Dove is generally resident and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. In Costa Rica it occurs year-round, although local movements may follow food availability or changes in rainfall and habitat conditions.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from April through August, possibly extending into October. The nest is a loose, fragile platform of grasses, fine twigs, and other plant material, usually placed 1–8 m above the ground in a tree or thorny shrub, but sometimes on buildings or other structures. Two white eggs are normally laid. Pairs may reuse nests and can make repeated nesting attempts during a favorable season.
value.dietFeeding: The Inca Dove feeds mainly on seeds and grains gathered from the ground. It eats seeds from grasses, herbs, flowers, and shrubs and may also take spilled grain at farms or seed offered at feeders. It usually forages by walking slowly through bare ground or short vegetation, sometimes tossing leaves or loose plant material aside with its bill to expose hidden food.
value.behavior: Inca Doves are often seen singly, in pairs, or in small flocks. They walk with a characteristic forward-and-back head motion while feeding and commonly perch or roost in trees and shrubs. When startled, they make a rapid, rattling flight that may reveal the chestnut underwings and white tail edges. During breeding, males defend territories, display with raised wings, and may confront intruding doves. Pairs commonly preen one another.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable, with increases or range expansion in some developed and open areas, including parts of North America. In Costa Rica, it has expanded southward and into additional settled areas over the past century.
